routes.description: Establish that compassion and other humane goods arise independently of religion, then show that religious doctrine, dogma, revelation, or institutional authority appropriates those goods while adding morally harmful conditions or obstructing reform.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if independently available human decency explains the admitted goods and representative doctrinal and historical cases show religion adding material harm without supplying a necessary, uniquely religious humane contribution.

motionBridge.description: Connect the motion to whether religion adds avoidable doctrinal harm to human goods that exist without it.

centralBridges.description: Establish that compassion, community, equality, and reforming concern can arise outside or prior to Christian doctrine.
Show that authoritative teachings or revelations introduce or entrench serious harms alongside claimed religious benefits.
Explain humane religious reform as movement away from specific harmful rules toward broader human compassion.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test claims of Christian humanitarian causation against prolonged conduct under Christian institutional power.
Use concrete cases such as slavery, subordination, and conquest to test proposed religious moral foundations.

routes.description: Distinguish corrupt religion from Christianity's governing sacred ideals, locate domination in a general human condition, and show how Christian anthropology and devotion supplied foundations and institutions for universal compassion, equality, and reform.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if Christian doctrines provide a coherent basis and historically consequential mechanism for humane ideals that cannot be reduced to unaided tribal concern, while apparent religious harms can be distinguished from or corrected by those doctrines.

motionBridge.description: Connect the motion to Christianity's capacity to originate, ground, and extend the humane ideals used to judge religious corruption.

centralBridges.description: Locate pride, violence, and domination in humanity generally rather than treating religion as their distinctive cause.
Ground equal human worth and moral obligation in divine love, the image of God, and the incarnation.
Trace sacred ideals into practices and institutions extending protection and compassion beyond kin, status, or tribe.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Show how Christianity contains standards for condemning corrupt religious power and interpreting difficult inherited practices.
Explain why moral condemnation requires a foundation stronger than present agreement or culturally contingent preference.

sections.title: The Governing Test: Prior Human Goods or Distinctive Religious Contribution
sections.rationale: This issue defines what the motion requires by testing whether acknowledged religious goods are uniquely generated by religion or are independently human goods burdened by harmful additions.

sections.title: Slavery, Abolition, and the Pace of Christian Reform
sections.rationale: Slavery supplies the debate's principal doctrinal and historical test of whether Christianity entrenched domination or furnished the anthropology and reforming trajectory that overcame it.

sections.title: Women, Family, and Christian Social Institutions
sections.rationale: The competing accounts of scripture, monogamy, and institutional change test whether Christian teaching constrained exploitation or imposed harmful subordination on women.

sections.title: Moral Grounding, Divine Love, and Equal Human Worth
sections.rationale: This issue concerns whether humane judgments can stand on shared human concern alone or require the Christian account of divine goodness, love, and persons bearing sacred worth.

sections.title: Conquest Narratives, Revelation, and Religious Violence
sections.rationale: The Canaan narratives provide a concentrated test of whether revelation authorizes grave moral harm or can be interpreted within a framework that ultimately prohibits religious violence.

sections.title: Universal Compassion and Its Historical Sources
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether concern for outsiders, enemies, and the weak is an ordinary cross-cultural human capacity or a distinctively Christian ideal made socially expansive through doctrine and institutions.
